title: Context plan
description: What one agent needs in order to perform one task correctly. NOT an execution plan: it holds no steps, no ordering and no implementation decisions. The context engine owns this document; the specialist owns the steps. Most fields are optional on purpose — a trivial task's plan is three lines, and inventing the rest is the failure mode this schema exists to prevent.

task.title: What was asked for, how big, and what kind of work it is
task.description: What was asked for, restated in one line.

summary.description: One line, in the user's terms, not the agent's.

type.description: The kind of work. Drives retrieval ranking and the verification contract.

size.description: Sets the context budget and how much of this plan is worth filling in. `trivial` means no plan is warranted — record the size and stop.

agent.title: Which single role owns it, why, and the near-miss it beat
agent.description: Who owns the work. One role. A chain is one plan per hop, not one plan with several owners. `selected_by` and `confidence` record how the owner was chosen, so a route can be explained after the fact.

reason.description: Why this role, in one line, tied to the deliverable the request asks for.

considered.description: Near-miss roles and the line that excluded them. Usually the role's own `not_for`. Fill this only when the call was close.

forced.description: True when the user named the role (/agent-<slug>). Routing did not happen and must not be second-guessed.

selected_by.description: Who made this selection. `forced` — the user named it. `recipe` — a recipe fixed it. `jev` — a configured decision engine chose it. `default` — the dispatcher's own method. Provenance, not authority: none of these values grants anything.

confidence.description: The confidence the decision engine reported, when it reported one. For diagnostics, policy and evaluation — not for the execution prompt, and never to be narrated as certainty. Absent means no engine produced one, which is the normal case.

capabilities.title: The capability ids the work needs — asked for before any skill id
capabilities.description: Capability ids this task needs, from catalog/skills.json. This is the bridge between the task and the skills: ask for a capability, then see which installed skill provides it.

skills.title: The task-relevant skills selected, each with the reason and whether it is actually installed
skills.description: The skills actually selected — one to five for ordinary work. A skill is here because a capability required it, never because it is installed.

reason.description: What this task needs that this skill supplies.

tier.description: Where the role's loadout puts it.

condition.description: For a conditional skill: the signal id from catalog/signals.json that admitted it.

status.description: `selected` — loaded. `substituted` — the first choice was absent and this one covers the capability. `unavailable` — named by the loadout but not installed; the role's own method carries the work.

substitutes_for.description: The unavailable skill id this one stands in for.

selected_by.description: Who made this selection. `forced` — the user named it. `recipe` — a recipe fixed it. `jev` — a configured decision engine chose it. `default` — the dispatcher's own method. Provenance, not authority: none of these values grants anything.

confidence.description: The confidence the decision engine reported, when it reported one. For diagnostics, policy and evaluation — not for the execution prompt, and never to be narrated as certainty. Absent means no engine produced one, which is the normal case.

stack.title: What the project is, with the file behind each claim, and which conditions that settles
stack.description: What the project actually is, and which conditional buckets that opens. Detection activates guidance. It never grants authorization.

detected.description: Each claim with the file it came from. A claim with no evidence path is a guess with formatting.

evidence.description: The path, and the substring if a content check decided it.

conditions.description: signal id -> outcome. `unknown` is a real and common answer; the signal's own `when_unknown` says what follows from it.

undetermined.description: What detection could not establish. Part of the result, not an omission.

retrieval.title: What to go and find in the workspace, and the question each search answers
retrieval.description: What to go and find in the workspace, and why. Queries, not results.

query.description: Identifiers, paths or phrases to search for.

context.title: What retrieval returned — ranked, deduplicated, capped, each with its provenance
context.description: What retrieval returned, ranked, deduplicated and capped. Every entry carries its provenance — why it is here, and how it matched.

reason.description: Which retrieval query brought it in, and what it is expected to answer.

match.description: How it matched. `expansion` means a strong result imported or referenced it — bounded, and the strong result is named in `via`.

via.description: For `expansion`: the path that led here.

rank.description: 1 = most relevant. Ordinal only. It is not a probability and must not be reported as one.

lines.description: The range actually read, e.g. "120-180". Absent means the whole file.

excluded.title: What was retrieved and then dropped, and why, so a wrong cut is visible
excluded.description: Retrieved and then dropped — by the cap, by deduplication, or as noise. Recorded so a wrong cut is visible rather than silent.

tools.title: Which servers are present, absent or unestablished — availability, never authorization
tools.description: MCP servers and host tools that materially help. Availability is a fact about the environment; it is never authorization.

status.description: `available` — its tools are present in this session. `absent` — named by the loadout, not present; the registry's `fallback` applies. `unknown` — not established.

reason.description: What it would be used for. An `absent` entry says instead which check cannot be performed.

selected_by.description: Who made this selection. `forced` — the user named it. `recipe` — a recipe fixed it. `jev` — a configured decision engine chose it. `default` — the dispatcher's own method. Provenance, not authority: none of these values grants anything.

confidence.description: How relevant a decision engine judged this server, when one was asked. Relevance only: it says nothing about availability and nothing whatsoever about authorization.

permissions.title: What authorization the work needs, and how each status is actually known
permissions.description: Authorization the work needs. The runtime owns permission and exposes almost none of it for inspection, so every entry carries how it is known. Never assert a permission from a role file, a skill or a detected stack — none of them grant anything.

verification.title: The evidence required before this is done, fixed before the work rather than after
verification.description: The evidence that must exist before this work is called done. Written before the work starts, so it cannot be lowered to match what happened to be produced.

check.description: The concrete check, e.g. "the original reproduction re-run after the fix".

skill.description: The verification skill that defines it, when one does.

status.description: Set at planning time to `required` or `blocked`. `blocked` names, in `basis`, the tooling that is missing — and the report then says the check was not performed rather than downgrading the claim.

budget.title: Roughly how much context this should spend, and on what
budget.description: Roughly how much context this task should spend, and on what. Approximate by design — the point is to prefer relevant context over a full window, not to count tokens precisely.

diagnostics.title: What this plan could not establish, and what was degraded
diagnostics.description: What this plan could not establish, and what was degraded: a recommended skill that is not installed, a server that is absent, a retrieval that found nothing, a condition left unknown. An empty list is a claim; do not make it falsely.

decision.title: Which engine made the bounded choices above, and whether it fell back
decision.description: Present only when something other than the dispatcher's own method decided. Diagnostics, not instruction: the specialist's work is identical whichever engine answered.

engine.description: `default` or the id of the engine that answered, e.g. `jev`.

provider.description: The transport the engine used. Never a credential, and never the variable's value.

fallback.description: True when an engine was attempted and the default answered instead. `diagnostics` says why.

registry_version.description: A digest of the candidate registries, so a routing result can be reproduced after metadata changes.

id.description: workspace-read, workspace-edit, command-execution, network-fetch, browser, external-write, deployment.

status.description: `known` — established, and `basis` says how. `unavailable` — established as withheld: plan mode gating writes, a call already refused. `unknown` — the runtime does not expose it, which is the honest default for most entries.

basis.description: The observation behind the status: "the user asked for the edit", "plan mode is active", "a Bash call was denied this session". Required whenever status is not `unknown` — and now enforced, not only asserted.
